intro.heading: You sent the new policy. Now you need to know it was understood.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: After a fall on the stairs, a manager rewrites the falls prevention policy. The new version asks for a different response after an unwitnessed fall. She uploads it, emails the team and pins a one page summary in the staff room. The team includes carers whose first language is not English, and the change is detailed. A week later three people have opened it and nobody has said a word. She cannot tell who read it, who understood it, or who is quietly unsure. Here is how that week plays out.

trail.text: The manager rewrites the falls prevention policy after a fall on the stairs.
She uploads it and emails the whole team.
A one page summary goes up on the staff room board.
Only three carers have opened the new version.
Some carers read English as a second language. A detailed change is easy to half follow.
Nobody asks questions. Nodding is not the same as knowing.
An email that was sent and a policy that was opened. Nothing about understanding.
After another fall: “What are you now meant to do first?” Three answers, three versions.

trail_close: Sending the policy was never the problem. The gap is between a policy update that went out and proof that each person understood it. Here is how CareStream closes it, in each carer's own language.

why.heading: Opening a policy does not show it was understood
why.sub: A changed policy only protects people if every carer does the new thing, not the old one.

cards.title: A word can hide a whole step
cards.body: A carer can know falls prevention well and still miss one phrase in a long document. That is a word gap, not a knowledge gap, and it is easy to confuse the two.

cards.title: Emails prove sending, not reading
cards.body: An email shows you sent it. CareStream records read sessions, such as time spent and scrolling, and a "Mark as read" tap. It does not record a signature or an acknowledgement.

cards.title: Old habits survive a change
cards.body: People keep doing what they did last month. Without a quick check on the change itself, the old way can carry on until an incident shows it.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We emailed the new policy. Why is that not enough?
items.a: An email shows it was sent. It does not show who opened it, still less who understood it. After a policy update, you can allocate a short check built from your own policies and see each person's answers.

items.q: How does a carer read the policy in their own language?
items.a: Your admin sets each person's first language, and an optional second. When they open a policy it is translated into their first language and kept for next time. The first time may show English while it translates, then it appears on the next open. The menus and buttons in the hub stay in English.

It is machine translation, not a professional human translator. It uses your own translation glossary, so terms you want kept as they are stay put, and carers can suggest a better wording that your admin approves. Treat it as a strong help for understanding, and do not treat it as a certified translation.

items.q: How do I check that people understood the change?
items.a: Allocate an adhoc module on the topic, such as falls prevention. Questions come to carers in their own language, and each answer is scored. A wrong answer is information, and it points to a gap in knowledge rather than a gap in vocabulary.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into their Follow-up tab in the Staff Hub and they get an email, at most once a day, in English. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: Will CareStream tell my team when a policy changes?
items.a: Not automatically. You decide who needs to know and allocate the module yourself. That keeps you in charge of who is asked what, and when.

items.q: Is this a read and sign register?
items.a: No. CareStream records read sessions, such as time spent and scrolling, and a Mark as read tap. It does not record signatures or acknowledgement. The questions are your evidence of understanding. See the compliance picture.

items.q: Can I try it, and does it cost anything?
items.a: Yes. Create a free account and try it for 14 days on a paid plan. Adhoc training and translation are on the paid plans, and the free plan is English only. See the pricing page for the plans, or register to start.

limits.heading: Honest about what this does and does not do

cards.title: It is not professional translation
cards.body: Translation is done by machine, with your glossary and approved staff suggestions. Nothing here is certified, and no human translator checks it. Safety critical wording is still worth a conversation.

cards.title: It does not notify staff when a policy changes
cards.body: You allocate the module and choose who gets it. Nothing alerts you to each wrong answer either, so the picture comes through the Knowledge gaps view and the Monday digest.

cards.title: Translation and adhoc training are on the paid plans
cards.body: The free plan is English only and does not include adhoc training. Hub menus and buttons, and the wrong answer email, stay in English on every plan.

items.q: What is policy translation in CareStream?
items.a: When a carer opens a policy, it appears in their first language and is saved for later. It is machine translation, helped by your own glossary. See the multilingual Staff Hub for the full picture.

items.q: How do you support a multilingual workforce in a care service?
items.a: Give people policies, lessons and questions in the language they think in, then check understanding with questions rather than assuming. Your admin sets each person's first language and an optional second, as described on the languages page.

items.q: Can a carer switch to a second language?
items.a: Yes, if your admin turns on allow switching. They can flip one lesson or question set into their second language with Read in their language. Their first language stays the default.

items.q: Does a wrong answer mean the carer is not good at their job?
items.a: No. It may be a missed word, a long sentence or a rushed read. That is why questions arrive in the person's own language, so a wrong answer points at knowledge and not at vocabulary.

items.q: Is the translation done by a person?
items.a: No. It is machine translation, with your own glossary and staff suggestions that your admin approves. We do not offer certified or professional translation. Read more in translating care policies.

items.q: What is a good policy update process for a care home?
items.a: Upload the new version, tell people what changed, then run a check for understanding. A short knowledge check on the changed topic shows who has taken it in. The four question framework helps you decide who needs more than a read.

items.q: What is a knowledge check, and how long should it be?
items.a: A short set of questions on one topic. Keep it to a few questions on the change itself. CareStream builds it from your own policies, and you can edit and preview it first.

items.q: Does CareStream record that staff signed or acknowledged the new version?
items.a: No. It records read sessions, not signatures or acknowledgement. Your evidence is the questions asked, the answers given and the lessons followed.

items.q: What do inspectors expect on staff training?
items.a: Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal they need to do their jobs. The CQC guidance on Regulation 18 says completion of training should be monitored, with prompt action when requirements are not met.

guide.heading: A practical way to roll out a changed policy to every carer
guide.lede: A policy update is only finished when people do the new thing. A good rollout checks understanding in a language each person is comfortable in, and does not rely on goodwill or a reminder email.

sections.h3: Keep the change small, then check it
paragraphs: Start by writing down what is actually different, in two or three lines. If the whole policy changed, say so, but a manager usually finds that only one or two steps are new. Questions on those steps tell you far more than questions on the entire document.
Then decide who needs it. A policy on falls matters to every carer, but a night team, an agency worker and a new starter may all need a different nudge.

sections.h3: A rollout that works for a mixed team
checklist: Upload the new version and say plainly what changed.
Allocate a short module on the topic, with a due date.
Let carers read in their first language, and offer a second language where it helps.
Review the most missed questions after a week and talk to the people who need it.

paragraphs: A wrong answer after a policy update is a signal that the message did not land, not a mark against the person. If several people miss the same question, change how you explain it. If one person misses it, a quiet conversation is usually enough.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the changed policy, the questions, the answers and the lessons together, so you can show that people understood the change as well as received it.
